restaurant-crm.title: Restaurant CRM & Booking Platform
restaurant-crm.summary: Booking system and CRM running daily in a restaurant in Graz.
restaurant-crm.result: In daily use at the restaurant, replacing the paid booking service: guests book online, staff manage the day from one screen.
restaurant-crm.context: A small restaurant with five tables needed online reservations, a menu it could edit itself and one place to manage guests — without a monthly SaaS fee and without handing guest data to a third party.
restaurant-crm.problem: The restaurant paid a monthly fee for a third-party booking tool that didn't fit how it actually worked, and its guest data lived on someone else's platform.
built: Public website in German, English and Ukrainian with menu, promotions, gallery and online booking.
Booking engine that picks the best-fitting table for the group size, respects visit length and turnover buffers, and prevents conflicts.
Admin CRM with reservations by day, table plan, menu and content editing, and role-based access.
highlights: Allocation rules modelled explicitly: table capacities, 60/90-minute visits by group size, 15-minute buffers and a last-slot cutoff.
Credentials authentication with JWT sessions; access checks enforced on every protected page.
German as the mandatory source language, with automatic fallback for English and Ukrainian content.

dealradar.title: DealRadar — marketplace deal finder
dealradar.summary: A Telegram bot that watches willhaben.at and kleinanzeigen.de and only sends the listings worth opening.
dealradar.result: Live and open to everyone, in four languages, running on AWS for about $12 a month.
dealradar.context: Second-hand marketplaces are full of accessories, wanted ads and junk. Checking a search by hand means scrolling through dozens of irrelevant listings, and a single average price says little about whether one offer is actually good.
dealradar.problem: Prices differ hugely between variants of the same product, so one blended average makes the expensive model look overpriced and the cheap one look like a bargain. AI on every listing would also get expensive fast.
built: Paste a search link or just type what you want: the bot builds a filter and notifies you about new listings and price drops.
A market scan that reads every page of a search and reports prices model by model, as a Telegram Mini App.
Feedback buttons under each notification that teach the filter what you do and don't want.
Free and Pro plans, invite links, a privacy page and one-command data erasure.
highlights: Deal scores come from per-model medians of the live market — the AI judges relevance and condition, never the price.
Rules first, AI second: a German marketplace lexicon drops most junk for free; only what passes is classified, in batches, with a cache and a daily budget per user.
Polite by design: one request per unique search per cycle, a per-host queue with backoff, and a health alert when a site's layout changes.
Core logic doesn't depend on Telegram or the LLM vendor; both sit behind ports, so the bot is tested end to end offline — 262 tests, strict TypeScript, CI on every push.
Infrastructure as code: Terraform provisions EC2, ECR, S3 + CloudFront and secrets in SSM; GitHub Actions deploys with no open inbound ports.

styleme.title: StyleMe — AI hairstyle try-on
styleme.summary: Upload a selfie and see yourself with a new hairstyle in seconds.
styleme.result: First MVP is live and publicly usable.
styleme.role: Solo — product, full-stack, architecture, DevOps and security
styleme.context: People want to see a haircut on themselves before committing to it. A consumer AI product also has to stay cheap per request and hard to abuse.
styleme.problem: Image generation costs real money on every request, so free usage needs limits that can't be bypassed from the browser.
built: Upload a photo, pick one of 40 preset styles, describe one in free text or use a reference photo, and get a generated result.
A free daily quota plus extra credits earned by watching an ad.
highlights: Image generation through Replicate, with the per-generation cost built into the quota design.
Quotas and rate limits enforced on the server, per IP and per user, in Redis — nothing is trusted from the browser.
Rewarded-ad credits protected against fraud: single-use server-issued nonce, minimum watch time, atomic redemption and a calculated worst-case cost ceiling.
Monorepo with a shared package as the single source of truth for types, Zod schemas and machine-readable error codes.
Unit, contract and Playwright end-to-end tests in CI; architecture decisions documented as ADRs.

englishlearn.title: EnglishLearn — adaptive learning platform
englishlearn.summary: An English course that decides what you should practise next, based on a model of what you actually know.
englishlearn.result: Pre-launch: the learning engine is built and tested; the student-facing app is in progress.
englishlearn.context: Most language apps show every learner the same sequence of lessons.
englishlearn.problem: A fixed sequence wastes time on what the learner already knows and moves on before weak spots are fixed.
built: A learner model that estimates what the student knows, predicts what they are about to forget and chooses the next exercise accordingly.
Planned next: an AI tutor and a diagnostic placement test.
highlights: Learner model combining Bayesian Knowledge Tracing, Item Response Theory, FSRS spaced repetition and Thompson Sampling.
Turborepo monorepo with Prisma, PostgreSQL and Auth.js; four interface languages.
Engine covered by an automated test suite.

media-processing-platform.title: Media Processing Platform
media-processing-platform.summary: An asynchronous media-processing backend with a Telegram bot as its first client.
media-processing-platform.result: Works end to end, including files over 1 GB; now in beta with a limited group of testers.
media-processing-platform.context: A Telegram bot that takes a link and sends back the processed media file — designed from day one as the core of a platform, not a one-off script.
media-processing-platform.problem: Long-running media jobs can freeze a bot, hit platform file-size limits and tie business logic to one messenger.
built: Send a link, watch live progress and receive the file in the chat, including files over 1 GB.
highlights: Clean Architecture with ports and adapters: Telegram is one adapter, so a web or REST client can be added without touching the core.
Heavy jobs run in a separate OS process that can be killed on timeout, so the bot never freezes.
Live progress streamed through Redis pub/sub — the processing layer knows nothing about Telegram.
Files up to 2 GB via a self-hosted Telegram Bot API server instead of the 50 MB public limit.
Secure by default: domain allowlist, no shell execution, sliding-window rate limiting; 181 tests and strict type checking.
